scenes.title: A BOAT COMES BACK
scenes.story: Dawn on the pier. A creel boat drifts in with its rope trailing. Nobody is aboard.
scenes.clue: The yellow barrel in the stern is chewed through, and both coats are still aboard.
scenes.prompt: What do you say to the men on the pier?
scenes.explanation: Present Perfect for a past event with a result now: has + taken. The sea is singular, and took is Past Simple.

scenes.title: TWO BOATS ARE MISSING
scenes.story: You ring the harbour bell. Doors open along the street. Men count the boats at the pier, then count them again.
scenes.clue: The brass bell rings over two empty spaces, and no engine answers from the Sound.
scenes.prompt: What do you say when the ringing stops?
scenes.explanation: Negative Present Perfect: have not + come. The auxiliary is have, never do, and it takes the past participle.

scenes.title: REGATTA WEEK STARTS FRIDAY
scenes.story: Provost Baird will not close the water. Regatta Week starts on Friday, and the whole village needs the money.
scenes.clue: The red buoy stays in the Sound, and no coastguard boat is in the bay.
scenes.prompt: How do you ask Baird about the coastguard?
scenes.wrong1: Do you have called the coastguard?
scenes.explanation: Yes/no questions put have before the subject, then the past participle. Never use do as the auxiliary.

scenes.title: THE WOMAN FROM OBAN
scenes.story: A car stops at the top of the slip. Dr. Maren Hoy carries a metal case down.
scenes.clue: The sonar case is new and unscratched, and she is younger than you expected.
scenes.prompt: What do you ask Dr. Hoy first?
scenes.correct: Have you ever dived in this loch?
scenes.wrong1: Ever have you dived in this loch?
scenes.wrong2: Have you ever dive in this loch?
scenes.explanation: Ever asks about any time up to now. It goes after the subject, before the past participle.

scenes.title: THE RING OF HORN
scenes.story: Dr. Hoy holds a jar up to the lamp. Inside is a black ring of horn, cut from something's beak.
scenes.clue: The black ring in the glass jar is bigger than anything in the Oban tanks.
scenes.prompt: What does Dr. Hoy say about the ring?
scenes.correct: I have never seen one this big.
scenes.wrong1: I haven't never seen one this big.
scenes.wrong2: I have never saw one this big.
scenes.explanation: Never already means not at any time, so have stays positive: have never + seen. Seen, not saw.

scenes.title: QUINN OPENS HIS SHED
scenes.story: Angus Quinn opens his shed. Yellow marker barrels hang along the wall. He turns one round, and you lift your radio.
scenes.clue: The yellow barrel on the wall is still swinging, bitten clean through the middle.
scenes.prompt: What do you say into the radio?
scenes.correct: Quinn has just shown me one.
scenes.wrong1: Quinn has shown me one just.
scenes.wrong2: Quinn has just show me one.
scenes.explanation: Just means a very short time ago. It goes between has and the past participle.
scenes.object: the yellow barrel on the wall

scenes.title: SHAPES ON THE SCREEN
scenes.story: Hoy lowers her sonar float over the reef. Quinn cuts the engine. Shapes fill the screen at once.
scenes.clue: The orange sonar float is barely wet, and the screen is full.
scenes.prompt: Hoy ___ the shapes on her screen.
scenes.explanation: ALREADY goes between HAS and MARKED, never between MARKED and its object. Hoy is one person, so HAS.

scenes.title: CUT CLEAN THROUGH
scenes.story: Hoy pulls a creel net over the rail. It is cut clean through, edge to edge. Quinn turns it over in his hands.
scenes.clue: The torn net hangs on the rail. Quinn stares at it and stays silent.
scenes.prompt: Quinn ___ yet about the net.
scenes.explanation: YET needs a negative here: HAS NOT + past participle. SPOKEN is the participle; SPEAKING is the -ING form.

scenes.title: ONE SEAL LEFT
scenes.story: Quinn takes the Selkie past the low rocks. One seal on the whole rock. Hoy counts twice, then lowers the binoculars.
scenes.clue: The last seal lies alone on the rock. Forty were here until Friday morning.
scenes.prompt: The rock has been empty ___.
scenes.explanation: A point in time takes SINCE: SINCE Friday. A length of time takes FOR: FOR two weeks.

scenes.title: SOMETHING TOUCHES THE HULL
scenes.story: Something long drags down the side of the Selkie and is gone. Quinn turns the wheel toward the old wreck.
scenes.clue: The scarred hull plate is still wet, and Quinn names the sound without looking.
scenes.prompt: Quinn ___ these waters for thirty years.
scenes.explanation: FOR gives a length of time up to now: HAS + past participle. HAS never takes FISHING, and the present cannot reach back.

scenes.title: THE MOUTH AT LOW WATER
scenes.story: You take the inflatable under the headland at low water. The roof drops to a hand above you.
scenes.clue: Quinn's boat is not at the mouth. The storm lantern shows wet oar marks.
scenes.prompt: Quinn ___ into the cave ahead of you.
scenes.explanation: Already for something that has happened before now; yet belongs in a negative or a question. Go becomes gone.

scenes.title: THE EMPTY DINGHY
scenes.story: Deep in the caves a dinghy turns slowly against the wall, half full of water. Nobody is aboard.
scenes.clue: The dinghy lamp is still burning, and nobody answers when you call.
scenes.prompt: The owner of this dinghy ___.
scenes.explanation: Yet goes at the end of a negative. Use has not plus the past participle come; came is Past Simple.

scenes.title: SHELLS ON THE LEDGE
scenes.story: The passage opens into a chamber. A dry ledge carries heaped shells and smashed creels.
scenes.clue: The broken creel is Quinn's. He lost it on Tuesday, in calm water.
scenes.prompt: The broken creel ___.
scenes.wrong1: has been here since two days
scenes.explanation: Since marks the point when something started; a length of time needs for. One creel takes has.

scenes.title: THE CAVE IS FILLING
scenes.story: The cave is filling fast. Quinn is aboard again, wet through. He turns the inflatable out towards the wreck.
scenes.clue: You came in two hours ago. The wet tide line is over your head now.
scenes.prompt: You ___.
scenes.correct: have been in here for two hours
scenes.wrong1: have been in here since two hours
scenes.wrong2: have been in here two hours ago
scenes.explanation: For measures a length of time. Since needs a starting point, and ago needs the Past Simple.

scenes.title: FOUR METRES OF WATER
scenes.story: The Selkie stops above the Morag. The trawler lies on her side in four metres of water. Hoy puts on a mask and goes in.
scenes.clue: The yellow barrel breaks the surface, and Hoy comes up the ladder behind it.
scenes.prompt: Hoy is back on board. She ___ down to the wreck.
scenes.explanation: Been is there and back; gone is still away. She is here. Went is not a past participle.

scenes.title: ELEVEN IN THE WATER
scenes.story: Quinn shows the scar. "The boat went down at night. Eleven of us were in the water. Something took them, one by one. Nobody believed me."
scenes.clue: The old harpoon head is worn smooth. Quinn's thumb sits in the same groove.
scenes.prompt: How long ___ that harpoon head?
scenes.explanation: How long asks for time from the past until now: have + you + had. In a question have comes before you.

scenes.title: OPEN BELOW THE WATER
scenes.story: You look down through green water. The side of the wreck is torn open. Quinn does not need to look twice.
scenes.clue: The brass porthole is green with twenty-eight years of growth. Quinn remembers that winter.
scenes.prompt: The Morag ___ in the winter of 1998.
scenes.explanation: A finished time like 1998 needs Past Simple. Present Perfect does not say when, so it cannot take a year.

scenes.title: RUN FOR THE CORRY
scenes.story: You reach the Corry. The whirlpool is flat and still. Quinn ties a rope around the capstan.
scenes.clue: The rope on the capstan is tight. Something below is pulling.
scenes.prompt: What does Quinn say about the rope?
scenes.explanation: The rope is singular: HAS + gone, never HAVE. "Went" is a past simple form, not a past participle.

scenes.title: IT COMES UP
scenes.story: A wet grey arm comes over the side of the boat. Dr. Hoy does not move. Nobody speaks.
scenes.clue: The arm over the side is thicker than a man and longer than the boat.
scenes.prompt: How do you describe the arm?
scenes.correct: The biggest thing I have ever seen.
scenes.wrong1: The biggest thing I have ever saw.
scenes.wrong2: The biggest thing I ever seen before.
scenes.explanation: After a superlative, Present Perfect with "ever": HAVE + seen. "Saw" is past simple, and HAVE can never be dropped.

scenes.title: THE LAMP GOES OUT
scenes.story: The engine stops and starts again. Quinn puts his hand flat on it. The Corry pulls at the boat.
scenes.clue: The engine stops and its lamp goes out. Three times now.
scenes.prompt: Which question do you ask about the engine?
scenes.correct: How many times has it stopped?
scenes.wrong1: How many times it has stopped?
scenes.wrong2: How many times have it stopped?
scenes.explanation: "How many" + HAS + past participle counts a result now. The question inverts: HAS IT. "It" never takes HAVE.

scenes.title: THE REGATTA LIGHTS
scenes.story: Regatta Week, and Baird keeps the water open. You take the quay wall for the night watch. Small lights swing above the moored boats.
scenes.clue: The harbour lamp shows a line of moored boats, every one of them empty.
scenes.prompt: Every skipper in the harbour ___ ashore.
scenes.explanation: EVERY + singular noun takes HAS + past participle. CAME is Past Simple, not the participle.

scenes.title: ONE LAMP STILL BURNING
scenes.story: The moored yachts go dark one by one. No engines, no shouts. Far out on the black water one small light is still burning.
scenes.clue: The last lit lamp is the only one left; Quinn started fishing here at fourteen.
scenes.prompt: Quinn says it is the first time the harbour ___ dark.
scenes.explanation: After THE FIRST TIME use Present Perfect, not a present form: HAS + past participle. WENT is Past Simple.

scenes.title: THE PONTOON LIFTS
scenes.story: The pontoon tilts under you. A rope runs tight from the deck down into black water. Your knife is out. The boats must go free.
scenes.clue: Three rope ends lie loose on the boards; the strained mooring rope is the fourth.
scenes.prompt: How many mooring ropes ___ tonight?
scenes.explanation: HOW MANY + HAVE + YOU + past participle counts a result now. Keep question order; the participle of CUT is CUT.

scenes.title: THE BARRELS GO OVER
scenes.story: You hold the rope. Hoy throws the third barrel over the rail. Quinn keeps the boat steady.
scenes.clue: The day is not over. Two barrels float behind. The yellow barrel is next.
scenes.prompt: Hoy ___ two barrels over the side today.
scenes.explanation: "Today" is not finished: HAS + THROWN. "Threw" needs a finished time, and "throwed" is not the participle.

scenes.title: THE LAST SHOT
scenes.story: You take the shot. The fourth barrel goes on. The line runs out fast and the boat swings round.
scenes.clue: The harpoon line is tight. All four barrels are still there.
scenes.prompt: So far nothing ___.
scenes.explanation: A result that stands now takes HAS + COME. "So far" does not take "came", alone or after HAS.

briefing.title: YOUR PRESENT PERFECT SEA CHART

cards.head: FORM · HAVE / HAS + PAST PARTICIPLE
cards.text: The tide HAS turned. I HAVE BEEN out and I am back; the ferries HAVE GONE and are still away.

cards.head: NEGATIVE · HASN'T / HAVEN'T + PARTICIPLE
cards.text: The fog HASN'T lifted, so the crews HAVEN'T slept.

cards.head: EVER / NEVER · ANY TIME UNTIL NOW
cards.text: HAVE you EVER touched one? I HAVE NEVER stood so close.

cards.head: JUST · ALREADY · YET
cards.text: Hoy HAS JUST arrived. Baird HAS ALREADY refused and HASN'T signed YET.

cards.head: SINCE + A POINT IN TIME · FOR + A PERIOD
cards.text: The boats HAVE been missing SINCE dawn, FOR eight hours.

briefing.note: A finished time takes the PAST SIMPLE: the boat WENT out at six. THIS WEEK is not finished, so it keeps the Present Perfect.

choices.title: WHERE THE WATER SPLITS
choices.story: Past the harbour mouth the channel divides. Hoy has the sonar ready. Choose where you search first.
choices.object: the channel marker where the water splits

routes.label: RUN FOR THE REEF
routes.note: Open water over the reef, where the creel boats set their nets.

routes.label: ENTER THE SEA CAVES
routes.note: Low water opens the cave mouths. The Selkie anchors off and waits.

choices.title: RUN OR STAY
choices.story: The tide turns at midnight. Quinn wants the Corry. Baird wants the regatta lights on. Choose tonight.

routes.label: RUN FOR THE WHIRLPOOL
routes.note: Quinn knows the slack water. The whirlpool is the kraken's ground.

routes.label: HOLD THE HARBOUR TONIGHT
routes.note: Two hundred people ashore, and the whole fleet moored and lit.

cover.title: KRAKEN: THE BLACK TIDE
cover.lead: You are Sergeant Isla Brodie, new to Kilmara and no friend of deep water. Two creel boats went out on the loch and their crews are still out there. The Provost will not close the water.
cover.small: Single player · B1 · two branching routes

endings.label: PRESENT PERFECT MASTER
endings.title: THE FLEET GOES OUT
endings.text: Four barrels held. The black tide has gone out of the loch. Quinn ties the Selkie up himself. At noon Baird sends the fleet out, and Kilmara works the Sound again.
endings.object: the brass harbour bell, bright at noon

endings.label: KRAKEN GONE
endings.title: QUINN COMES ASHORE ALIVE
endings.text: The barrels come up. The thing under them does not. Quinn sits on the slip, wet and alive. His boat has gone to the bottom. By evening the loch is quiet.
endings.object: the yellow barrel washed up on the slip

endings.label: BARRELS MISSING
endings.title: IT GOES DOWN UNMARKED
endings.text: You did not get four barrels into it. The black tide slides back into the Corry with nothing to follow. No skipper will leave the pier while it is down there. Read the chart again and take the boat out.
endings.object: the single yellow barrel left on the pier

endings.label: OUT OF CHANCES
endings.title: THE SELKIE IS NOT BACK
endings.text: The berth where the Selkie ties up is empty water. The lifeboat has been out since dark, and nobody has found anything. At first light nobody else will go out. The story is not over.
endings.object: the lifeboat searchlight sweeping the water

critique.problem: Friday runs backwards. `provost` says "Regatta Week starts on Friday" (Friday is ahead). An hour later on the REEF branch, `reef3` says "Forty were here until Friday morning" and the correct answer is "since Friday" (Friday is behind). Chapter 4 `night1` then says Regatta Week is happening. A REEF player meets both statements within minutes of each other; the only reading that saves it is that day 1 IS Friday, which makes "has been empty since Friday" nonsense on a Friday afternoon.
critique.fix: Move the seal colony off Friday and off cave3's Tuesday. reef3 clue: "The last seal lies alone on the rock. Forty were here on Monday morning." correct: "since Monday"; wrong1: "for Monday"; wrong2 unchanged. Explanation: "A point in time takes SINCE: SINCE Monday. A length of time takes FOR: FOR two weeks."

critique.problem: Quinn and the Selkie are in two places on the CAVES branch. `sound` puts you aboard the Selkie with Quinn and Hoy ("Choose where the Selkie searches first"). `cave1` then says "Quinn's boat is not at the mouth" and the correct answer is "Quinn has already gone into the cave ahead of you" — so the boat you just arrived on has vanished and its skipper has overtaken you. `cave4` has him leaving in the inflatable, and `wreck1` opens with "The Selkie stops above the Morag", a boat nobody has been aboard for four scenes.
critique.fix: cave1 clue: "Quinn's punt is tied off at the mouth. The storm lantern shows wet oar marks." (the Selkie is left outside with Hoy; Quinn rowed in). cave4 story: "The cave is filling fast. Quinn is aboard again, wet through. He runs the inflatable out to the waiting Selkie."

critique.problem: The explanation style is split down the group seams. Chapter 1 (drift, bell, provost, hoy, jar, shed), the whole CAVES branch and all three wreck scenes write grammar tokens in lower case ("has + taken", "have never + seen", "Been is there and back"). The REEF branch, the CORRY branch, the NIGHT branch and Chapter 5 write them in CAPS with quoted forms ("ALREADY goes between HAS and MARKED", "\"Went\" is a past simple form"). Every player crosses at least one seam. The house rule and the most recent shipped RPG (frankenstein-green-prometheus-rpg: "The negative uses BE, not DO: he + ISN'T + going to + leave") are CAPS.
critique.fix: Convert the thirteen lower-case explanations to CAPS tokens. e.g. drift: "Present Perfect for a past event with a result now: HAS + TAKEN. THE SEA is singular, and TOOK is Past Simple." wreck1: "BEEN is there and back; GONE is still away. She is here. WENT is not a past participle." Also normalise the tense names — CAPS-group writes "past simple form" (corry1) where everyone else writes "Past Simple".

critique.problem: Two defects in one item. (a) The distractor "threw" is correct English — "Hoy threw two barrels over the side today" is standard; the learner is being marked wrong for an acceptable sentence, which is the distractor-is-also-correct class that cost this repo eight preposition items. (b) It makes the last two questions of the game the same question: `barrels` is has thrown / threw and `last` is has come loose / came loose, back to back, both Present Perfect vs Past Simple, and slot 18 already owns that contrast. "threw" is also the only five-character option in a field of ten- and eleven-character ones.
critique.fix: Move the gap onto the time expression, which is what slot 17 is for. prompt: "Hoy has thrown two barrels over the side ___." correct: "today"; wrong1: "yesterday"; wrong2: "at six this morning". explanation: "TODAY is not finished, so Present Perfect fits. YESTERDAY and AT SIX are finished times: they need Past Simple."

critique.scene: briefing card 3 (against jar) and card 1 (against drift)
critique.problem: The chart hands over two answers before the game starts. Card 3 reads "I HAVE NEVER seen one." and `jar`'s correct option is "I have never seen one this big." — the same string plus two words. Card 1 reads "The loch HAS taken them." and `drift`'s correct option is "The sea has taken them." — same verb, same object, same shape. The briefing is on screen immediately before question 1.
critique.fix: Change both examples to verbs the eighteen items never use. Card 1: "The tide HAS turned. The lamps HAVE burned all night." Card 3: "HAVE you EVER touched one? I HAVE NEVER been so close." (Card 4's "Hoy HAS JUST arrived. Baird HAS ALREADY refused." is fine — it narrates the chapter without printing an answer string.)

critique.scene: endings master / missing / failed (against provost, night1, cover)
critique.problem: Three endings resolve a harbour closure that never happens anywhere in the script. The cover says "The Provost will not close the harbour", `provost` says Baird will not close the water, `night1` says "Baird keeps the water open". Then `master` says "At noon Baird lifts the order" — an order nobody issued — and `missing` and `failed` say "The harbour stays shut" / "The harbour is shut".
critique.fix: The scene graph is fixed, so fix the endings. master: "…At noon Baird sends the fleet out himself, and the boats go back on the water." missing: "…The harbour stays empty. Read the chart again and take the boat out." failed: "…No boat leaves the pier, and the story is not over."

critique.problem: The same item twice in different words, on the CAVES path. `bell` (slot 2, negative) is correct "They haven't come back." / wrong "They haven't came back." `cave2` (slot 8, YET) is correct "has not come back yet" / wrong "has not came back yet". Same verb, same negative, same participle error. Slot 8 is supposed to be paying for YET, and half of it is re-running slot 2.
critique.fix: Change cave2's verb and let YET carry the item. prompt unchanged; correct: "has not turned up yet"; wrong1: "has not turned up still"; wrong2: "has not turn up yet". Clue must stop pre-answering it: "The dinghy lamp burns on its hook, and both oars are shipped."

critique.problem: The named grammar point never decides the answer. Options are "has not spoken" / "has spoken" / "has not speaking". The clue says "Quinn stares at it and stays silent", so "has spoken" is eliminated by the story, and "has not speaking" by surface shape. A learner who has no idea that YET needs a negative still scores. cave2, the parallel slot-8 item, does test it properly.
critique.fix: Make the wrong option a real YET error that the story cannot eliminate: correct "has not spoken"; wrong1 "did not speak"; wrong2 "has not spoke". Explanation: "YET needs the Present Perfect negative: HAS NOT + SPOKEN. Past Simple cannot take YET."

critique.problem: In every one of the twenty-five items the correct option is never the longest of the three — it is shortest or tied-shortest thirteen times and never strictly longest. "Never pick the longest" is a free elimination on all eighteen questions, and it survives whatever order the builder shuffles them into. Combined with the fact that one distractor is a past-simple-for-participle error in thirteen of the eighteen items on a given path, several questions can be solved by surface shape alone.
critique.fix: Make the correct option the longest in at least four items. Worked examples: reef3 correct "since Monday morning" against "for Monday morning" and "since two weeks"; cave4 correct "have been in here for two hours now" against "have been in here since two hours"; corry2 wrong2 shortened to "The biggest thing I ever seen." so the correct option is longest.

critique.problem: Subject agreement is the eliminable distractor in five of the eighteen items on a path — drift wrong1 "The sea have taken them", reef1 wrong2 "have already marked", wreck3 wrong2 "have sunk right here", plus corry1 and night1, whose whole slot (14) it is. Slot 1 and slot 14 end up testing the same thing in the same frame: singular noun + HAVE + participle, and singular noun + HAVE/HAS + past simple.
critique.fix: Leave agreement decisive only at corry1 and night1. drift wrong1 → "The sea has taked them." (over-regularised participle, matching the slot's stated point). reef1 wrong2 → "has already mark". wreck3 wrong2 → "has sank right here".

critique.problem: The same beat and the same verb twice, and every player gets both. `jar` is "I have never seen one this big." (slot 5) and `corry2` is "The biggest thing I have ever seen." (slot 15) — both are a character reacting to size with EVER/NEVER + SEEN. Ten questions apart, it reads as the writer reaching for the same line twice.
critique.fix: Keep the superlative line at corry2 and change the verb at jar: correct "I have never held one this big."; wrong1 "I haven't never held one this big."; wrong2 "I have never hold one this big." Explanation: "NEVER already means not at any time, so HAVE stays positive: HAVE NEVER + HELD. HELD, not HOLD."

critique.problem: Two problems. "has fishing" is not a real B1 learner error — it is nonsense, which bible rule 2 forbids. And the prompt hands the learner "for thirty years" ready-made, so slot 10 (FOR + a period) is never actually chosen on the REEF path; the item ends up re-testing slot 1's HAS + participle. cave4, the parallel item, does make the learner pick FOR over SINCE and AGO.
critique.fix: wrong2 → "has fish" (bare verb after HAS, a genuine error, parallel to "has not speak"). If you want slot 10 to bite on both branches, move the marker into the options: prompt "Quinn has fished these waters ___." correct "for forty years", wrong1 "since forty years", wrong2 "forty years ago".

critique.problem: Quinn's age does not add up across branches. reef4 says he has fished these waters for thirty years; wreck3 puts the Morag on the bottom twenty-eight years ago in 1998, with Quinn one of eleven crew in the water; night2 says he started fishing here at fourteen. That makes him forty-four now and sixteen on the night of the sinking, which sits badly against the bible's "old creel fisherman" with a lifetime's grudge. A REEF-then-WATCH player gets both numbers.
critique.fix: reef4 prompt → "Quinn ___ these waters for forty years." Forty years from fourteen makes him fifty-four now and twenty-six in 1998 — a crewman, and an old man today.

critique.problem: "Nobody is aboard." appears verbatim in both, and both scenes are the same reveal: a small boat found with its crew gone. A CAVES player gets the identical sentence and the identical beat at question 1 and question 8. There is also a wider tic — five sentences in one playthrough open with Nobody (drift, cave2 story, cave2 clue "nobody answers when you call", wreck2 "Nobody believed me", corry2 "Nobody speaks").
critique.fix: cave2 story: "Deep in the caves a dinghy turns slowly against the wall, half full of water. The thwart is empty." Vary at least two of the remaining Nobody openings.

critique.problem: The bitten barrel is revealed twice in Chapter 1, five questions apart. drift's clue already says "The yellow barrel in the stern is chewed through"; shed's clue then plays it as the discovery — "bitten clean through the middle" — and shed's whole beat (Quinn turning a barrel round, you reaching for the radio) depends on it being new information. "clean through" also turns up again at reef2 ("cut clean through, edge to edge").
critique.fix: Hold the damage back at drift: clue → "The yellow barrel in the stern hangs by a stub of rope. Both coats are aboard." Then shed's bitten barrel lands as the reveal it is written to be, and reef2 keeps "clean through" to itself.

critique.problem: Hoy disappears for a quarter of the game on the CAVES branch. The route card promises "Hoy has the sonar ready. Choose where the Selkie searches first", and then four consecutive scenes mention only Quinn and you; she reappears at wreck1 putting on a mask. The sonar, the thing the choice was sold on, is never used on that branch at all.
critique.fix: Put her in the chamber scene: cave3 story → "The passage opens into a chamber. Hoy lights a dry ledge of heaped shells and smashed creels." And soften the route card: sound story → "Past the harbour mouth the channel divides. Hoy has the sonar ready. Choose where you search first."

critique.problem: The route note sells the harbour choice on "The regatta boats are lit. Two hundred people on the water." The scene it leads into says the opposite one screen later: night1's clue is "a line of moored boats, every one of them empty" and its correct answer is "Every skipper in the harbour has come ashore." The stake the player chose evaporates.
critique.fix: WATCH note → "Two hundred people ashore, and the whole fleet moored and lit." The moored, lit, empty boats are then what night1 shows, and the people are on the quay where the player is.

critique.problem: The two branch-final scenes are written as the same moment. corry1's clue is "The rope on the capstan is tight. Something below is pulling." night3's story is "A rope runs tight from the deck down into black water." The plates differ (whirlpool capstan by day, pontoon cleat by night), but the text is the same sentence, and a player who replays to take the other branch reads it twice.
critique.fix: Push corry1's wording onto the drum and the load, not the tightness: clue → "The rope is smoking round the iron drum. Something below is taking it." Leave night3 as the bar-tight rope.

critique.problem: "still burning" describes a single small lamp over dark water in both — cave2's clue ("The dinghy lamp is still burning") and night2's story ("one small light is still burning"). One is on the CAVES branch, the other on the WATCH branch, so a replayer meets the same image and the same two words on the second run.
critique.fix: night2 story → "…Far out on the black water one small light still shows." The masthead lamp plate is unaffected.

critique.problem: The chart does not cover three things the questions actually test. (a) The contracted negative HASN'T / HAVEN'T + participle is never modelled, yet bell, reef2 and cave2 test it and five distractors across the game are built on it — card 4's "Nobody HAS left YET" is a positive verb form, not a negative. (b) BEEN vs GONE is a whole slot (wreck1) with no card, and the note's "not HAS GONE" is the only place GONE appears, used for a different purpose. (c) The unfinished time period (barrels: today) has no card; the note gives only the finished-time half of the contrast.
critique.fix: Card 2 carries the negative without losing result-now: "The coastguard HASN'T come, so the boats stay in." Card 1 carries been/gone alongside the form: "Hoy HAS BEEN down to the wreck. Quinn HAS GONE out to the Corry." Extend the note: "A finished time takes the PAST SIMPLE: the boat WENT out at six. TODAY and THIS WEEK are not finished, so they keep the Present Perfect."

critique.problem: The panel contradicts itself on the count. The story has Hoy throwing the third barrel over the rail right now; the clue says "Two barrels float behind. The yellow barrel is next" — so the third is simultaneously going over and still to come. (The prompt's "two barrels … today" is the only part that is consistent.)
critique.fix: clue → "The day is not over. Two barrels float behind the boat." Drop "The yellow barrel is next." — the plate already has a barrel going over the rail.

critique.problem: The last run happens twice at different times of day. `barrels` is daylight — "The day is not over", "today". `master` ends at noon, which fits. But `complete` says "By morning the loch is quiet" and `failed` opens at "Dawn" with the lifeboat "out since two", both of which read as a night action ending the following morning.
critique.fix: complete → "…By evening the loch is quiet." failed can keep dawn if the search runs overnight, but say so: "…The lifeboat has been out since dark. Nobody has found anything."

critique.problem: The same error type in consecutive questions, with the same closing rule in both explanations. bell wrong1 is "They don't have come back." and provost wrong1 is "Do you have called the coastguard?" — both do-support with the perfect — and both explanations end on "the auxiliary is have, never do" / "Never use do as the auxiliary." Question 3 teaches nothing question 2 did not.
critique.fix: bell wrong1 → "They not have come back." (a real B1 omission error), and end its explanation on the participle instead: "Negative Present Perfect: HAVE NOT + COME. The negative needs the auxiliary HAVE, and CAME is Past Simple."

critique.problem: The missing-boat arithmetic does not close. The cover says the sea has taken two boats; drift brings one boat back in to the pier with two coats aboard; bell then rings "over two empty spaces" and counts the boats twice. If the drifted boat is in, only one berth should be empty — as written there are three boats in play and two crews accounted for.
critique.fix: Drop the number from bell's clue and let the title carry it: "The brass bell rings over the empty berths, and no engine answers from the Sound." Or keep the count and leave the creel boat adrift in the bay rather than alongside: drift story → "A creel boat turns in the bay with its rope trailing. The thwarts are empty."
